Priscilla Alvarez (@priscialva)

What "voluntary departure" means legally: no formal removal order, which theoretically makes future legal return easier. But Vera's researchers are clear that for people departing from detention under these conditions, calling it voluntary misrepresents the coercion involved.

Geography shows up here too. Texas (12,400) and Louisiana (5,400) led voluntary departure orders in the Sep. 2025–Feb. 2026 period. Both states have high concentrations of detained immigrants and historically restrictive immigration courts.

Vera's researchers also found that newly appointed, inexperienced immigration judges, hired under threat of dismissal, are disproportionately assigned to detained dockets and are granting voluntary departure at higher rates than veteran judges.

The spike tracks specific policy changes: the July 2025 ICE memo declaring detained immigrants ineligible for bond hearings. Once you remove the possibility of release pending your case, the calculus for detained people shifts dramatically.
More than 70% of those granted voluntary departure during Trump's second term were in immigration detention when they requested it, far higher share than under Biden.

Immigration judges issued more than 80,000 "voluntary departure" orders from January 2025 through March 2026, at least 7x the number issued in the final 15 months of the Biden administration. "Voluntary" is doing a lot of work in that phrase.

What we don't yet know: how many of the 330 new hires are agents vs. administrative or support staff, and what specific enforcement targets are being assigned to each field office. Federal purchasing records show where people are going; they don't show what they're tasked to do.

DHS Secretary Mullin has said the agency is deliberately keeping a lower profile: moving quietly, letting agents work without media attention. A hiring surge paired with reduced visibility is an operational choice, that is harder to track and report on than a high-profile raid.

The ACLU of Ohio found that before 2025, only two Ohio counties had formal ICE cooperation agreements. That number has grown. More 287(g) agreements = more pipeline for identifying people through local jails = more arrests that look like CAP data.

The national deployment prioritizes Texas (49 new agents, the largest single-state allocation). Ohio is part of a broader build-out, not a specific escalation. But the infrastructure being laid here, field office capacity,enforcement agreements, is what enables future operations.

"Operation Buckeye", in Columbus, resulted in 240 arrests over six days. The Dispatch's analysis of Deportation Data Project records found fewer than 7% of those arrested had a criminal record, despite ICE framing the operation around "the worst of the worst criminals."

ICE is deploying 330 newly hired officers and staff across 40+ states and Puerto Rico, including 5 new employees each at its Westerville and Brooklyn Heights field offices in Ohio. Ohio has already been a test case for what this surge looks like in practice.

Carlos Della Valle returned home to his wife Angela and son after nearly 9 months in detention. Today at 3:00 PM eastern he will speak with Nick Valencia *LIVE*! 

Watch here: piped.video/@nickvalencianew….

My longer analysis on what the Deportation Data Project reveals about interior enforcement priorities is on Substack: austinkocher.substack.com 
Read:  doi.org/10.21670/ref.2601179

What the data don't yet tell us: actual removal counts. The Trump administration hasn't published detailed deportation statistics, only arrest figures. Arrests and removals aren't the same thing and the gap in transparency is significant.

It's not just one administration's rhetoric and it reflects something structural: when you set a quantity target (3,000/day), you inevitably arrest people who weren't previously enforcement priorities.

The biggest driver has always been the Criminal Alien Program (CAP), which targets people already in local jails. But arrests classified as "located" and "non-custodial" meaning community & workplace jumped in 2025. Only 33% of "located" cases involve a criminal conviction.
